strengths: Novel conceptual framing distinguishing 'Galtonian' (initialization-time) vs. post-hoc fingerprints, providing fresh perspective on LLM attribution
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 58 models, 6 transformation types, and 2 model architectures (LLaMA, Qwen) with near-perfect LeafBench performance
Convincing empirical demonstration that untrained models exhibit seed-dependent token biases that persist through training, with proper statistical testing (p < 0.01)
Strong robustness across various parameter-altering transformations (instruction tuning, PEFT, quantization, merging, distillation) where prior methods degrade
Thorough ablations in Section 5.1 with multiple statistical tests (t-test, Mann-Whitney U) showing consistency across different evaluation paradigms
Addresses domain shift scenarios where prior fingerprinting methods fail, demonstrating persistence under continual training on divergent corpora
weaknesses: Practical relevance severely limited: initialization seed is not part of standard model provenance, unlike training data or architecture; real model-theft scenarios typically involve fine-tuned variants of the same base model rather than different-seed initializations
Extremely weak effect sizes (rank correlation ~0.006, explaining <0.0036% of variance) despite statistical significance—raises serious concerns about practical robustness and real-world deployability
Shallow mechanistic understanding: why these biases exist, whether they depend on initialization scheme details, and how they scale to 70B+ parameter models all remain unexplored

Critical hyperparameter choices completely unjustified with no ablations: fingerprint size m, number of random inputs n, significance level α=0.01, and identity index selection method (why argmin over argmax or both?)

Methodological issues undermining statistical rigor: (1) non-standard p-value averaging over 10 trials rather than single hypothesis test, (2) no multiple comparison correction across 20+ tests per table, (3) arbitrary p-value → score conversion breaks statistical calibration for AUC/KS metrics

Limited experimental scope: all experiments use small-medium models (≤14B), standardized HuggingFace training, and controlled initialization; real-world variation in hardware, distributed training, and frameworks unexplored
Overstated claims about prior method failures (Table 3): some baselines achieve 0.999+ performance on TinyStories; 'failure' characterization is misleading

Design choices poorly justified: why Kendall-Tau over Spearman? Why pseudo-token embeddings rather than vocabulary tokens? Why only argmin identity tokens when Figure 1 shows both argmax/argmin are informative?
Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity analysis on m, n, α; no comparison of correlation measures; no evaluation on truly large models (70B+) or distributed training scenarios

Conceptual framing issues: 'Galtonian fingerprint' and 'birth-to-lifecycle' claims are misleading—biases depend on RNG implementation details, not intrinsic properties; method never demonstrated on untrained models alone

strengths: Novel 'Galtonian' fingerprinting framework that targets initialization-intrinsic properties rather than post-training artifacts, providing a clean conceptual contribution
Striking empirical observation that untrained models exhibit seed-dependent token selection biases that persist measurably through training, well-demonstrated in Figure 1

Extremely comprehensive experimental evaluation: seed-level discrimination across multiple architectures, 58-model LeafBench covering 6 transformation types, robustness under domain shifts, and all-stage verifiability
Strong empirical results achieving 0.992 AUC and 0.992 KS statistic while matching/exceeding baselines (Intrinsic: 0.995, ICS: 0.994) across practical scenarios
Statistical rigor using proper hypothesis testing with calibrated p-values and null distributions, enabling principled lineage verification compared to similarity thresholds
Well-specified Algorithm 1 with clear justifications for design choices (Kendall-Tau correlation, softmax normalization, identity index extraction)
Demonstrated robustness to aggressive parameter modifications (fine-tuning, PEFT, quantization, merging) where existing methods degrade substantially
weaknesses: Lacks theoretical justification for why cross-entropy training preserves initialization biases; no mechanistic explanation for persistence of small correlations (≈0.006) or principled understanding of when/why the method works
Critical design choice of pseudo-random embeddings over vocabulary sampling is buried in footnote; missing ablations comparing these approaches or justifying this decision

Unclear practical advantage in realistic scenarios: LeafBench results (0.992 AUC) only marginally differ from simpler baselines like Intrinsic (0.995), and unique capability (seed discrimination) may not address copyright protection concerns
Insufficient ablation studies: fingerprint size m impact unexplored, sensitivity to number of random sequences n not analyzed, identity token stability and selection mechanism underdocumented
Requires white-box model access and computation over many random sequences; computational cost not discussed and adversarial robustness against initialization manipulation not addressed
Reported p-values (10^-260) exceed numerical precision; multiple comparisons across tables without correction; threshold sensitivity (α=0.01) not explored
Main controlled experiments limited to small models (12-layer); scalability to large foundation models (70B+) unclear; lack of theoretical complexity/distinguishability bounds
Practical motivation underdeveloped: seed-level discrimination addresses problem of uncertain relevance for copyright auditing, as initialization seeds are not typically considered IP

strengths: Compelling core insight: The observation that initialization-dependent biases persist through training is interesting and well-motivated, distinguished from post-hoc fingerprinting methods.

Rigorous statistical framework: Principled hypothesis testing with empirically validated null distributions (both analytical and simulation-based), along with theoretical stability analysis (Lemmas C.1-C.2).

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive experiments across multiple scales (up to 3.9T tokens), model families (LLaMA, Qwen), and realistic scenarios (LeaFBench with 65 models and 6 transformation types), with consistent positive results.

Strong empirical performance in target regime: Achieves perfect or near-perfect detection throughout training from initialization onward, and maintains robustness under domain shift (TinyStories vs The Stack).
Careful reproducibility and documentation: Algorithm clearly presented, extensive appendices with theoretical proofs and implementation details, code promised for release.
weaknesses: Severe practical limitations: Method requires white-box access to logits/hidden states with no feasible black-box variant. In realistic threat models, stolen models are deployed as black-box APIs. Authors acknowledge but inadequately address this fundamental constraint.

Questionable practical significance: Achieves AUC 0.992 vs. 0.994 for baselines on realistic LeaFBench scenarios, showing no meaningful improvement. Additionally, initialization seeds have no copyright status (authors' own admission), limiting applicability to realistic model theft scenarios where trained models are stolen, not seeds.

Limited novelty in methodology: Core algorithm is straightforward (select bottom-m dimensions, compute rank correlations, hypothesis test). Main contribution is observational (initialization biases persist) rather than methodological. No novel statistical or computational techniques.

Incomplete understanding of persistence mechanism: While Section 3 shows empirically that biases persist, lacks formal characterization of why they survive 3.9T tokens of training. Invokes Li et al. (2026) on representation contraction but doesn't explain relative ranking preservation through massive weight updates.

Missing adversarial evaluation: No analysis of robustness to intentional fingerprint evasion attacks. Model merging experiments (Table 7) show degradation to AUC 0.959, suggesting signals can be diluted. No evaluation of adaptive defenses or weight-space perturbations.

Weak underlying signal: Correlations in Figure 2 are <0.01 in magnitude (acknowledged as 'weak'). Requires 2M+ forward passes per verification. Extreme p-values (10^-260) suggest either overfitting to null or trivial separation—contradicting 'weak signal' claims.

Statistical concerns with p-value usage: Converting p-values to similarity scores (1-p) for AUC is 'not fully aligned with statistical meaning' per authors. Exponential scaling of p-values doesn't translate to linear similarity thresholds, undermining AUC calculations.

Unrealistic experimental settings: Section 5.1 trains from scratch with identical data/order but different seeds—not representative of real copyright scenarios (independent fine-tuning with different data). Limited evaluation on cross-scale robustness (Table 14 shows variable performance).

Insufficient theoretical grounding: Sample complexity n = Ω(log d_out / γ²) requires unknown bias margin γ a priori. No guidance for setting hyperparameters on new architectures. Gaussian approximation for null justified primarily empirically, not theoretically.
